In the case of the Airport Spur, our calculations indicated that the overestimate is relatively minor due to the dominant influence of 1-94 traffic. The heaviest main-line traffic volumes may often be the best basis for estimating pollutant concentrations, while in other cases, treating all traffic in lanes crossed by the wind vector (drawn with an angle of 10° to the most heavily traveled lanes of traffic) may show that the air quality impact is acceptable despite the overestimate. In either case, the most appropriate traffic volumes would be those expected at the points where the 10° wind vector in a scale drawing crosses the various lanes, not those at the points to which the perpendicular distance measurements are made as were used in the Airport Spur Air Quality Report (see page B-22). However, this difference in traffic figures did not have a major impact on carbon monoxide values calculated in the case of the Airport Spur.
The Airport Spur Air Quality Report shows a misunderstanding of several points in the state Indirect Source Rules and DNR procedures for implementing them which should be cleared up if this air quality report is to serve as a model for future air quality reports. Notes at the bottoms of figures 50-52 refer to total receptor exposures in excess of 75% of the carbon monoxide standards as "violations" under DNR rules. This is not the case. The 75% criterion is used only in reviewing indirect source notices of intent to determine whether a proposed project should be approved without further review or made an affected facility. This supplies a margin of safety when simple screening techniques are applied to determine whether a national ambient air quality standard will be violated. If it is necessary to make a project an affected facility prior to approval or disapproval pursuant to NR 154.05(5), the air quality impact of the project will be evaluated with a more sophisticated model which incorporates additional data more accurate for the specific project under investigation than the values assumed in the screening technique. A second cri erion, significant degradation, is also applied in determining whether t . Department's action on a notice of intent should be to approve a soject or make it an affected facility. If the screening technique indicates that building a proposed project will increase the one-hour maximum carbon monoxide concentration by seven parts per million or more or the eight-hour maximum by two parts per million or more, then the project is made an affected facility, and the more sophisticated model is applied to determine more accurately whether these increments may be exceeded. If the more detailed analysis indicates that either increment will be exceeded, then a public hearing is called pursuant to NR 155.06(4) to determine the public attitude in the affected area toward permitting the predicted degradation. If the Department determines, as a result of the hearing, that a majority of the affected persons oppose permitting the significant degradation, then the project will be disapproved or issued a conditional approval designed to reduce project-caused degradation to less than the seven parts per million and two parts per million increments. If the Department determines that a majority of the affected persons favor the project as proposed despite the predicted degradation, then the project will not be disapproved solely because it causes significant air quality degradation.
